proof_nl: Let x be any real number, and set m = floor(x). By the defining property of the floor function, m is an integer, m <= x, and m is the greatest integer with this property. Suppose for contradiction that x >= m + 1. Then m + 1 is an integer and also m + 1 <= x. But this contradicts the maximality of m, since m + 1 > m is a larger integer still not exceeding x. Hence the assumption is impossible, so x < m + 1. Substituting m = floor(x), we obtain x < floor(x) + 1. Because x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.
solver_summary: Fix x and let m = floor(x). If x were at least m+1, then m+1 would be an integer not exceeding x, contradicting that m is the greatest integer <= x. Therefore x < floor(x)+1 for all real x.
vetter_reason: The proof directly establishes the standard floor bound x < floor(x) + 1 for an arbitrary real x. The argument is logically sound, matches the lemma statement exactly, and uses only the defining property of floor.
